turns.q:
Your response was: "I mean... I looked through it. There were some parts that felt familiar, some that didn't quite. I'm not sure I'm the right person to say whether it all makes sense — it depends a lot on who would normally use this. I suppose some things stuck with me a bit more than others — there was something near the bottom of one of the screens, some kind of action I think, though I couldn't quite tell what it was for. I couldn't say much more than that without thinking about it more."

We want to understand what you meant by "there was something near the bottom of one of the screens, some kind of action I think, though I couldn't quite tell what it was for", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The "Continue Shopping" button located in the lower section of the layout.
B) The "Place Order" button positioned at the bottom of the screen.
C) The legal disclaimer text regarding Terms of Service and Privacy Policy at the very bottom.
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: If I had to pick... probably B? I think. Though I'm not sure that's exactly it — it might be closer to another option, depending on how you're defining it. It's more of a general feeling than a specific thing. Other people might not even notice.

turns.q: What kind of work situation or real-world scenario would bring you to a screen like this?
turns.a: I'm not sure I have one specific moment in mind. It's more of a... recurring thing, I suppose. When the team needs to process something quickly and there's not much time for setup. Though I'm not sure that's specific enough.

turns.q: What were you trying to verify or confirm about the order process when your eyes landed on that "Place Order" button?
turns.a: I suppose just... complete the transaction. Get it submitted. I don't usually think of it as a 'job' — it's more like a step in something larger. Someone else usually handles the follow-up.

turns.q: How would you know this specific button placement succeeded in making the transaction feel fast and effortless?
turns.a: I'd know it worked if... nothing went wrong, I suppose. If a confirmation appeared and nothing needed to be corrected. That's what success looks like for this kind of thing.

turns.q: What is it about the button's appearance—specifically its fill, color, or border—that makes it hard to identify as the primary action?
turns.a: I mean... it was just a small thing. The button wasn't as prominent as I expected. Most of the time I'd figure it out. It's not a blocker, exactly.

turns.q: Is it the lack of a solid color fill that makes it hard to see as a button, or is the color itself too similar to the background?
turns.a: The problem is visibility, really. The button to submit — the 'Place Order' button — didn't look like a primary action. It looked like a label. So I spent time looking for something that was already there, just... not visible enough.

turns.q: When you look at the "Place Order" button, what specific visual property—such as the lack of a solid fill, the color choice, or the border style—makes it blend into the background?
turns.a: The button was gray on a gray background with very small text — 12 pixels, I think. For the primary action on the screen, that's basically invisible. I couldn't tell if it was meant to be interactive, if it was disabled, or if I was just overlooking it. The barrier is the contrast. To remove it: give the 'Place Order' button a solid fill color that actually stands out from the background, and increase the text to something legible — 16 pixels minimum. That's the change. Everything else on the screen was fine.
